newsitem.title: JAPAN: Matsushita profit seen closing gap with rival Sony.
newsitem.headline: Matsushita profit seen closing gap with rival Sony.

text.p: Profit growth at Matsushita Electric Industrial Co, Japan's lumbering electronics giant, is finally picking up speed and may soon close the gap with nimbler rivals like Sony Corp and Sharp Corp, analysts say.

They said that in the current business year Matsushita will continue to rack up strong sales of cellular phones, batteries and various computer-related products which have helped it recover from a consumer electronics slump in the early 1990s.

They added that Matsushita should also outperform most of its competitors in sales of audio-visual products and household appliances as well, despite intensifying price competition in these sectors and the prospect of a shrinking domestic market.

"Matsushita is getting more aggressive in the planning and development of consumer electronics," said Masahiro Ono, analyst at Credit Lyonnais Securities (Japan). "It could increase its market share this year."

Hideki Watanabe, analyst at Nikko Research Centre, added: "Companies like Sharp Corp and Sanyo Electric Co have fallen victim to Sony Corp's onslaught in the market for digital audio-visual products, but Matsushita would stay in the gainers' camp."

Matsushita Electric, which sells under the National and Panasonic brands, will unveil on Thursday its forecast for the current business year, along with final results for the 1996/97 business year ended on March 31.

For 1996/97, Matsushita predicted in December that it would post 120 billion yen ($1.05 billion) in group net profit, citing a strong showing in the computer and telecommunications sectors, now the company's biggest business area.
Financial analysts say they expect the company to meet its forecast and are now focusing on prospects for the current year, which ends in March 1998.
Their forecasts for growth in Matsushita's group net profit this year ranged from 18 percent to 35 percent, for a total of 140 billion yen ($1.22 billion) to 170 billion yen ($1.49 billion).

This is more than a six-fold increase from four years ago, when Matsushita was struggling under a consumer electronics slump, but still well below the peak profit of 259 billion yen ($2.27 billion) achieved in 1990/91.
Rival Sony Corp, by contrast, rang up a record group net profit of 139.46 billion yen ($1.22 billion) in 1996/97 and forecast a further rise to 160 billion in 1997/98.
Nikko's Watanabe expects Matsushita's sales in the computer and telecoms sectors to grow 15 percent during the year, aided by fast-rising sales of hard disk drives and CD-ROMs.
Sales of batteries will rise 10 percent, reflecting a surge in demand for lithium-ion batteries used in mobile phones and personal computers.
Sales of household appliances like refrigerators and televisions are expected to show a more modest increase of 3.1 percent, Watanabe said.

"The computer and telecoms sector will stay strong, but household appliances could lose steam in the second half of this year reflecting slower figures for housing construction," said Kazuya Yamamoto, analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research.

In early March, Matsushita predicted that Japan's consumer electronics market would shrink three percent in fiscal 1997/98 to 5.1 trillion yen ($44.7 billion), as price competition with imports heats up.
